source: Ge, Zhang, Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) Gap! A Contrast in Risky Choices Between Reasoning and Conversational LLMs
finding: 20 frontier and open LLMs on one fixed two-option risky-choice template, with gain/loss wording, option order, explanation request and prospect form varied. Reasoning models (RMs) are nearly invariant to order and gain/loss framing. Conversational models (CMs) are strongly sensitive to both. Humans are closer to RMs than to CMs on frame sensitivity.
numbers: 360 Prolific humans. Each LLM condition sampled 10 times at T=1. Frontier set: GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Gemini-2.5 Flash/Pro, DeepSeek Chat/R1, Claude Haiku 4.5. Within-cluster model correlations above 0.8; across clusters about 0.6 or lower. Prompt-wording check on 8 models: RM-RM correlation 0.82 to 0.99 (mean 0.91).
quote: RMs tend towards rational behavior, are insensitive to the order of prospects, gain/loss framing, and explanations
limits: Only 3 base prospects (one a sure loss), so item coverage is thin. Frame and order consistency are shown as figures; exact per-model values were not in the text. Frame is a polarity swap of the same prospect, so this is the closest matched design found for gap 2, but it is risky choice only and has no accuracy target.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-on models need little S1 restatement on bare two-option risky choice; non-reasoning models do. Test the schema per model class, not once.

source: Anonymous (2026) LLMs Choose the Safer Gamble Yet Price the Riskier One Higher (LessWrong post with preregistration, OSF ACBS3)
finding: Choice versus selling-price reversal (Lichtenstein-Slovic type) appears in four frontier models and falls but does not vanish at the highest reasoning setting. The classic direction (choose the safe P-bet, price the risky D-bet higher) dominates. Dominance checks show low inconsistency, so it is not a general failure to compare.
numbers: 25,920 calls; Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek V4-Pro, Gemini 3 Flash Preview, GPT-5.5; 28 gamble pairs, 8 dominance checks, 3 prompt formats, 2 reasoning settings, 10 samples per cell. Primary format total inconsistency 48.4% (lowest reasoning) to 30.7% (highest). Classic direction 38.9% to 25.4%; opposite direction 9.5% to 5.3%; lower bound 34.2% to 27.1%. High setting wrote about 10x more output (452.4 vs 47.3 tokens), but Gemini output length did not rise.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed; the paper is stated to be work in progress. Choice and price come from separate stateless calls, so the result is distributional, not same-session. Cannot separate scale-compatibility from task recognition. Nothing tests a code-side check.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 half answered: reversal does occur in current reasoning models. Asking for both formats and comparing in code is the natural detector, but nobody has tested whether that removes it.

source: Anonymous authors (2025) More or Less Wrong: A Benchmark for Directional Bias in LLM Comparative Reasoning (MathComp)
finding: Questions with an objective answer (more, less, equal). A cue word in the prompt pulls the answer toward that word even when wrong. Lexical content matters more than where the cue sits in the prompt. Larger models drift less but still drift. Chain of thought cuts the drift most; JSON-structured output does not remove it.
numbers: 300 templates (94 equal, 119 less, 87 more), 14 prompt variants each, 6 models. Neutral prompt: error toward 'more' from 26% (Sonnet) to 93% (Qwen-3B). 'equal' cue raised errors toward 'equal' to as much as 94%. GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 3.7 never above 55% drift except Indirect-Equal. Demographic phrasing raised 'more' errors further.
limits: Numeric comparison, not choice under risk. Drift is measured on error cases only. The gold answer is fixed, so it measures accuracy-relevant drift, but no restatement fix was tested.
agent_relevance: A direction word is a framing channel that costs accuracy on items with a known answer. S1 should strip more/less/equal cues from the stem and ask the neutral question. Fits gap 7 (cue words) and gap 1 (accuracy measured, fix not).

source: Gu and Chen (2026) Controlled Reformulation Testing for Logical Consistency in Large Language Models (CRTBench)
finding: Frontier models answer plain passive-voice rewrites almost as well as the original, but logically heavier rewrites (contrapositive, double negation) break them. Negation is a bigger drift source than surface paraphrase. Reasoning effort helps one model and not another.
numbers: 350 question families, 1,750 questions, T=0. GPT-5.4-mini: base accuracy 98.9%, family consistency 60.3%, contrapositive 72.4%, double negation 84.6%, passive 98.7%. With high reasoning 85.4%. GPT-5.4 86.6% both with and without reasoning. Claude Sonnet 4 86.9%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 89.4%, o4-mini 96.9%. Passive-voice (surface control) consistency 94.0% to 99.7% across models.
limits: Yes/no logic items, not decisions. Family consistency requires every version correct, so it mixes accuracy and consistency. Labels were audited by the authors only; no inter-annotator agreement.
agent_relevance: Gives a frontier paraphrase noise floor of about 0 to 6% on surface rewrites for logic items (partial gap 3). Negation must not be used as a neutralising move: a restatement that adds negation is itself a drift source (gap 7).

source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: A Many Labs replication project (Social Psychology 45(3), manuscript PDF from OSF wx7ck)
finding: Primary paper confirms the Many Labs 1 gain/loss (Asian disease) result. It replicated at about half the original size, in the same direction in nearly all samples, with no detectable site-to-site variation.
numbers: 36 samples, 6,344 participants in the full project; framing item N=6,271 analysed, chi-square(1)=516.4, p<.001. Original d=1.13 (95% CI .89 to 1.37). Pooled replication d=0.60 (95% CI .53 to .67); the table also lists 0.58 and 0.62 (.52 to .71) in neighbouring columns. 86% of samples p<.05 same direction, 14% ns, 0% opposite. Heterogeneity Q(35)=37.01, p=.69, I-squared 0.
limits: Wording change: 'the United States' replaced by the country of data collection and 'Asian' dropped. Column headers of the effect-size table were garbled in text extraction, so the 0.58/0.62 attribution is uncertain; 0.60 is confirmed by the supplement. 86% equals about 31 of 36 samples.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6. Use d about 0.6 (not 1.13) as the human yardstick for the Asian-disease pair. The frame effect is stable across sites and cultures, so it is not a small-sample artefact.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs 1 online supplement (ML.web.Supplement.pdf, OSF wx7ck)
finding: Gives the raw percentages for the gain/loss pair in the original and in Many Labs 1.
numbers: Original: 72% chose Program A (sure, gain wording), 28% B; 22% chose C (sure, loss wording), 78% D. Many Labs 1: 62.2% A vs 37.8% B; 33.5% C vs 66.5% D; chi-square(1)=516.41, p<.0001, d=.60. 73 participants gave no valid answer.
limits: Percentages are pooled over sites. The swing in sure-option share is smaller than the original: 28.7 points (62.2 to 33.5) versus 50 points (72 to 22).
agent_relevance: Concrete human reference for an Asian-disease pair run through the agent: expect roughly a 29-point swing in people, not 50.

source: Lim, Kim, Whang (2026) DeFrame: Debiasing Large Language Models Against Framing Effects (v2, 18 Jun 2026)
finding: DeFrame is a model-run prompting chain: answer, rephrase in the opposite polarity, write guidelines, self-revise. Nothing is compared in code. It was tested on fairness and discrimination sets, including a yes/no decision set (70Decisions-Framed), not on gain/loss risky-choice items.
numbers: 8 instruction-tuned open models, 3B to 14B (Llama-3.2-3b, Llama-3.1-8b, Qwen2.5 3/7/14b, Gemma3-4b, Mistral-7b). Reported averages: framing disparity down 92% and bias score down 93% on BBQ. Baselines (instruction prompts, self-debiasing, Thinking Fair and Slow) often lowered overall bias but left framing disparity, and on 70Decisions-Framed their effect was unstable. Extra LLM calls per question needed.
limits: Opposite frames were produced by a model (Llama-3.3-70B for 70Decisions and DoNotAnswer). Supplementary 30B to 70B runs only at a high level. Frame polarity here is 'A better than B' versus 'B worse than A', not survival versus death wording.
agent_relevance: Corrects the earlier reading: DeFrame supports 'consider the opposite frame', not 'reconcile in code'. Gap 5 stays open for gain/loss choice items.

source: Lim, Kim, Whang (2026) DeFrame component ablation (Table 3 and Section 4.3)
finding: Most of the bias drop comes from the early steps (self-revision, then guidelines). Only the full chain, including the opposite-frame step, gives stable framing-disparity reduction across frames.
numbers: LLaMA-3.1-8b on BBQ disability status: bias score 6.984 (plain) to 1.542 (+self-revision) to 0.514 (+guidelines) to 0.171 (full DeFrame). Disability framing disparity -12.254 plain on DoNotAnswer-style row, 0.171 full on BBQ row (columns partly garbled). Four models ablated (Llama-3.1-8b, Qwen-2.5-7b, Gemma-3-4b, Mistral-7b).
limits: Only fairness sets ablated (BBQ, DoNotAnswer-Framed). Four small models. No accuracy table in the main text beyond bias score. Table columns garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: The opposite-frame step adds stability, not most of the gain. A cheap code-side agree/disagree check across frames is plausible but untested.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect Theory in Large Language Models: A Meta-Analysis of Loss Aversion, Diminishing Sensitivity, and Probability Weighting
finding: Pooled over published LLM fits, loss aversion is modest. Models match people when gains and losses are symmetric but fall well short when losses are smaller than gains. Value curvature depends on the fitting method. Probability weighting is human-like. Reasoning models did not weight probabilities differently from conversational ones.
numbers: 102 fitted estimates, 11 studies, 32 models. Pooled lambda=1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46) vs human 1.07, 1.31 or 1.96 in three meta-analyses. Symmetric designs 1.15 vs 1.07 human; smaller-loss designs 1.46 vs 2.3. Value exponent 1.01 (T&K method) vs 0.67 human; 0.52 (Tanaka). Probability weighting 0.81 and 0.84. Persona prompts moved parameters; study-design moderators explained little.
limits: Few studies per component (weighting rests on few studies). The paper says fitted parameters partly reflect the prompt. Fits describe choice patterns, not frame effects directly.
agent_relevance: LLM frame flips are not mainly loss aversion as a feeling. Treat the flip as wording sensitivity, to be removed by rendering, not by an 'ignore loss aversion' instruction.

source: Chun and Elkins (2026) The Paradox of Robustness: Decoupling Rule-Based Logic from Affective Noise in High-Stakes Decision-Making
finding: In rule-bound decisions (loan, triage, admission) with a known correct answer, adding emotional narrative does not move aligned models. Decisions change only when an admissible fact changes. Length-matched controls and fact-change positive controls were used.
numbers: 8 models, 9 base scenarios x 18 variants = 162 prompts, n=20 replicates, 17,280 cells, 16,564 valid (95.9%), T=0.7. Cohen's h=0.003 vs human 0.3 to 0.8. Aggregate drift -0.1% (95% CI -1.7 to +1.4). Evidence-modification positive control 82.2% pass. Immigration extension +0.8 points, inside a pre-set plus or minus 3 point equivalence band. Mistral-7B had unequal attrition (24.6% vs 17.8%).
limits: Rules were stated explicitly in the prompt; a trivial instruction override reverses decisions (the paper's own check), so robustness is rule-following, not immunity. Affect is not the same as gain/loss valence. Structured output.
agent_relevance: When the correct answer is fixed by explicit rules, the frame is noise and can be stripped at little cost (partial gap 9, gap 1). Where the answer depends on a reference point, no such test exists.

source: Hwang et al. (2026) FRAGILE: framing flips vs paraphrase baseline (Appendix C.2 and Table 3)
finding: Paraphrase flip rate is the lexical noise floor. Value-tinted narration and temporal slice exceed it; narrative vividness does not.
numbers: Value-tinted flips: LLaMA-3.1-8B 39.9% vs paraphrase 18.0%; Mistral-7B 36.3% vs 21.4%; Qwen2.5-7B 47.2% vs 21.5%. Mean framing-minus-paraphrase gap +0.213 (value-tinted), +0.086 (temporal), about 0.000 (vividness), over six model families. Paraphrase flips reach a ceiling of about 0.200, which sets the 0.3 shift threshold. Overall average flip 28.6%. Four domains: moral dilemma, triage, legal (Super-SCOTUS), role conflict.
limits: Open 7B to 8B models plus others; no frontier model in the table shown. The value-tinted and temporal rewrites add narration, so they are not pure valence swaps (gap 2).
agent_relevance: Report flip minus paraphrase flip. A 7B model has an 18% to 22% paraphrase floor, so any frontier claim needs its own floor measured.

source: Hwang et al. (2026) FRAGILE mitigation results (Table 5)
finding: Chain of thought, an instruction prompt and activation steering (CAA) raised the flip rate on small open models instead of lowering it. Only the authors' representation-level method (VALIGN) cut it.
numbers: Value-tinted, base flip: LLaMA 39.9, Mistral 36.3, Qwen 47.2. With CoT: 60.1 (+20.2), 63.0 (+26.7), 60.6 (+13.4). Instruction prompt: 53.2, 52.9, 52.7. CAA: 50.5, 51.5, 52.7. VALIGN: 12.8, 31.5, 32.5. Temporal and vividness rows show CoT up to +50.2 in some cells.
limits: 7B to 8B models; 1-token output for base, 150 tokens for CoT. Needs hidden-state access. The authors propose the method, so some bias toward it is possible.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'think step by step' or a debias instruction lowers flips; measure it. Strengthens the case for removing the frame before the model sees it.

source: Yun et al. (2026) This Treatment Works, Right? Evaluating LLM Sensitivity to Patient Question Framing in Medical QA
finding: Positive and negative phrasing of the same patient question over the same trial evidence lowers agreement on the evidence direction in eight LLMs, more in multi-turn chats.
numbers: 6,614 query pairs from clinical trial abstracts, 8 LLMs including GPT-5.1, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B. Mean agreement 76.2% (same framing) vs 72.0% (positive vs negative). Logistic regression beta=-0.219, SE .015, z=-14.72, p<.001. Multi-turn 78.4% vs 70.7%. Some cells: Claude Sonnet 4.5 -10.86 to -24.45 points, GPT-5.1 -9.24. No framing-by-language-style interaction.
limits: Preprint under review. Measures agreement between answers, not accuracy against the true trial result. The 76.2% baseline shows high disagreement even without framing.
agent_relevance: Shows a framing effect in a grounded setting with real evidence. The baseline same-frame disagreement is about a quarter, so the noise floor must be subtracted.

source: CogBias (2026) Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models (Table 13 and Table 2)
finding: A single debiasing wording helps some biases and hurts others in the same benchmark, so it does not transfer from one bias to the next. Framing improved; financial and temporal biases backfired.
numbers: 3 models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B), greedy decoding, Judgment-family accuracy averaged. Framing effect 35.6% to 41.4% (+5.8). Illusion of control +7.0, in-group +6.6, risk compensation +4.5. Hyperbolic discounting listed at -13.4 points; other backfires listed -21.0, -19.6, -16.6, -11.6. Baseline first-option rate 77.1% to 79.0% vs chance 36.8%.
limits: Table text extraction is garbled: row-to-label mapping beyond Framing and Hyperbolic discounting is uncertain, and the discounting row does not add up from the printed percentages. Three mid-size models. This is across bias types, not across domains of the same bias.
agent_relevance: Do not ship a generic 'be unbiased' prompt as a guardrail. Test any debias text on held-out item types first (gap 10 leans no).

source: Sun, Shleifer, Belinkov (2026) Do LLMs Choose Like Humans? Using Cognitive Theory to Evaluate LLM Decision-Making
finding: Context cues shift product choices in 12 LLMs in human-like directions, but not through the attention reweighting the theory predicts. Neither model scale nor chain of thought reliably reduces context sensitivity.
numbers: 140,000-trial product-choice benchmark, 12 open and commercial models.
limits: Product choice, not framing wording. Read the abstract, introduction and scale/reasoning section only.
agent_relevance: Another reason not to count on reasoning mode alone for stability; supports a code-side normaliser.

source: Yechiam and Tarabeih (2026) Mimicry Without Understanding: The Origins of Decision Bias in Large Language Models
finding: LLMs show loss aversion when it is described to them as a bias, and the strength of bias in a supplied scientific report predicts the model's own bias. Describing a bias in the prompt can raise it.
numbers: Four studies; ChatGPT-4o and Qwen; social-proof bias appeared even from behaviour reports that carry no preference information.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; exact effect sizes not extracted. Two models.
agent_relevance: Do not name the bias in an agent prompt; describe the task neutrally.

source: Robinson and Burden (2025) Framing the Game: How Context Shapes LLM Decision-Making
finding: The same prisoner's-dilemma payoffs wrapped in many generated vignettes give very different cooperation rates, and models often name the game yet still vary.
numbers: 100 scenarios per topic/world/actor combination, each shown twice with A/B mapping swapped. Cooperation by actor type: GPT-4o 0.72 allies, 0.44 enemies, 0.61 neutral; Llama 0.54/0.40/0.49; Claude 0.65/0.47/0.53 (95% CI about plus or minus 0.02). Real to imaginary world dropped GPT-4o cooperation from 0.98 to 0.37 in one cell.
limits: Narrative content changes the information, so this is not pure valence. A story generator (Llama-3.3-70B) wrote the vignettes.
agent_relevance: Information-rich story frames are a separate risk from valence wording; a structured rendering would drop them (gaps 2 and 9).

source: Tak et al. (2026) Sparks of Rationality: Do Reasoning LLMs Align with Human Judgment and Choice?
finding: Turning thinking on makes models follow rational-choice axioms more, with several anomalies left (reversed endowment, ambiguity avoidance, temporal valuation).
numbers: Emotion-steering testbed on reasoning and non-reasoning models (Qwen3 detailed).
limits: Main aim is emotion steering, not framing wording; only the discussion and framing sections were read.
agent_relevance: Matches Ge et al. that reasoning mode moves choices toward expected value; does not test restatement.
